Specialized bikes and team Quick-Step officially ended one of the most significant partnerships in road racing Monday.

Both the U.S. bike behemoth and the long-running Belgian team confirmed Monday the end of an 18-year collaboration that brought the so-called “Wolf Pack” more than 800 victories.

Beginning in 2007, the partnership put the Specialized logo on top of the biggest races in the world and helped develop some of the most popular road bikes on the market.

The split marks the end of an era in professional cycling.

The collaboration between the brand and the team was one of the longest, most successful partnerships in the peloton.

Quick-Step riders won cobblestone monuments, Tour de France stages, and world titles on various iterations of the Tarmac, Shiv, and Venge. Riders like Tom Boonen, Mark Cavendish, and Remco Evenepoel are among the superstars who forged their palmarés on the brand’s bikes.

In return, the team helped Specialized refine some of its most successful models sold to the mass market .

Cavendish and Evenepoel are known to have been particularly active in developing its sprint and TT bikes, respectively.

The collaboration began in 2007, paused in 2010 and 2011, and has continued since 2012.

The news that the end was nigh was first reported , though not confirmed, in April.

Separate social media posts by both Specialized and Soudal Quick-Step on Monday made it official.

“After nearly two decades together, we’ve celebrated some of the sport’s most iconic moments, including victories in monument classics, grand tours, world championships, and countless stage races,” Specialized wrote on an Instagram post Monday.

“Thank you to the riders, staff, management, and fans who helped make this partnership so memorable and wishes Soudal Quick-Step and AG Insurance-Soudal continued success in the years ahead.”

It will be all change for the team currently known as Soudal Quick-Step in 2027.

The team will ride Merida Bikes and be known as Soudal Safety Jogger.

The Belgian flooring company Quick-Step steps down from its title sponsorship of the team for the first time in 24 years this winter.

Meanwhile, Merida will return to the peloton after it was last seen in 2025 with Bahrain Victorious. The Taiwanese manufacturer owns a 35 percent stake in Specialized.

The partnering women’s team AG Insurance-Soudal will also switch from Specialized to Merida in 2027.

With the Quick-Step team off the books, Specialized will tighten its focus on its ongoing partnerships.

The California-based brand will continue to invest in its partnerships with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, FDJ United-Suez United, SD Worx Protime, and the Specialized Factory Racing off-road superteam .

Demi Vollering, Remco Evenepoel, Keegan Swenson, and Lotte Kopecky will be its biggest-name athletes going forward.

MTB star Kate Courtney will also ride Specialized on the road after she made her bombshell move to FDJ United Suez this summer.

Tim Merlier won Quick-Step’s last race on a Specialized bike Sunday at the Eneco Tour. The Belgian super-sprinter gave his bike an affectionate tap after he blasted across the finishline.

“I think it is my 80th professional victory. I don’t know how many I have achieved on a Specialized [57 – ed], but since I started riding this brand of bikes, I’ve achieved many victories,” Merlier said at the finish Sunday.

“I’m very proud that I can finish this season with a victory for Specialized,” he said.

It was a suitably winning end to one of the winningest, most recognizable partnerships in pro road racing.

Grand tour winners, former world champions, and one of USA’s hottest talents will make career-defining transfers this winter.

Richard Carapaz, Giulio Ciccone, Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Andrew “AJ” August are the headline names making moves in a wildly busy transfer window that’s already seen Tom Pidcock get a superteam and Lidl-Trek go transfer crazy.

These five blockbuster moves promise the riders more freedom, leadership opportunities, and career progression. They offer the teams victories from Paris-Roubaix through the Tour de France.

Broken contracts, bizarre motivations, and troubled teams accompany some of these biggest moves of 2026-2027.

Here’s all you need to know about the five biggest transfers in the men’s peloton, as of October 20.

Stay tuned for a similar feature on some whopper contracts in the women’s sport.

For Carapaz: How does Richard Carapaz benefit by moving to NSN Cycling Team?

If you’ve got an answer, please let us know.

This feels like a sideways, or maybe even a backward move for one of the top-ranked riders in the world.

EF Education-EasyPost isn’t the best GC team in the world, but it’s been good enough to put Carapaz into the top-4 of a grand tour for three years in a row. Plus, it allowed its biggest rider the flexibility to roam free. Stage hunting, the KoM classification, GC – nothing was off-limits for Carapaz at EF.

What does NSN have to offer Carapaz (beyond a bigger paycheck)?

The Swiss-registered squad was a sprint-focused team in its debut 2026 season.

It’s bolstered its climbing division with Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt for 2027, but is still short on the climbing support Carapaz might need if he wants to go big at the Tour de France.

Beyond that, Carapaz might not get such a long leash at an ambitious team that clearly wants to break into GC racing. Here’s hoping he can keep bringing the panache.

For NSN Cycling Team: The answer is obvious – the team gets possibly the most exciting racer in the world. Carapaz will bring the team results, charisma, and guaranteed TV time.

Luring Carapaz from EF was the heist of the season , and by far the biggest transfer in the men’s peloton so far.

Carapaz broke his contract with EF to join NSN.

There’s no rumor of bad blood between the Ecuadorian superstar and the American team that gave him free rein over his racing ambitions. It just supported him through one of the best seasons of his career.

EF boss Jonathan Vaughters confirmed this week to Escape Collective that he’s suffering a budget crunch – something already evident in the exodus of talent leaving the team this winter and its sparse recruitment policy.

Maybe NSN made Carapaz an offer he couldn’t refuse, and one that Vaughters couldn’t match. The likelihood of a buyout fee would have made it a reluctant no-brainer for the impoverished American team.

For Ciccone: Giulio Ciccone will be a great white shark at Pinarello-Q36.5, having been one of many fish in an overflowing pond at Lidl-Trek.

The exuberant Italian will join Tom Pidcock as one of the ultimate bigs at Pinarello-Q36.5, which is rapidly emerging as one of the most audacious, ambitious teams in the bunch.

How Ciccone and Pidcock divide the calendar and their ambitions is another matter. Scheduling two top riders with such similar skill sets won’t be simple.

For Pinarello-Q36.5: Ciccone could have won GP Québec, the European championships, and Il Lombardia in the last month. When combined with Pidcock and Mauro Schmid, Pinarello-Q36.5 will have the ultimate triple-threat on suitably punchy parcours.

And if Pinarello-Q36.5 has Ciccone, Pidcock, and Schmid divide and conquer, they’ll be drowning in the UCI points they need to hit the WorldTour in 2029.

Ciccone was signed with Lidl-Trek through 2029. However, the 31-year-old was reportedly rubbed the wrong way by the recent management overhaul and identity shift at his long-time team. The Italian was a close ally of former team boss Luca Guercilena, who appears to have been squeezed out of his role in the team’s structural upheaval.

The overload of GC racers at Lidl-Trek no doubt improved Cicco’s mood, either.

This seems to have been an ugly divorce. The statements from Ciccone and Lidl-Trek confirming their contract termination couldn’t have been frostier.

For Ganna: Filippo Ganna needed a reboot, bad. The towering Italian has huge potential, and it’s been going untapped.

Sure, Remco Evenepoel is unbeatable against the clock right now, but Ganna’s proven he can be a lot more than just a time trialist. Remember his forays into bunch sprinting? Or his barnstorming breakaway antics at the 2020 Giro?

Aside from his spectacular win at Dwars Door Vlaanderen, Ganna lost his road-racing chops this season.

Ganna must see a move to Lidl-Trek as a new chapter.

New management, new motivation, and a team committed to classics racing and sprinting might restore the true “Top Ganna.”

For Lidl-Trek: Lidl-Trek must have watched the Italian track pursuit team and liked what it saw. Just imagine Ganna leading out his Italian pursuit teammate Jonathan Milan at the Giro d’Italia?! Bellissimo .

Ganna will bring Lidl-Trek a leadout man de-luxe and a heavyweight addition to its already hulking classics squad next year.

Ganna, Milan, Mads Pedersen, and Mathias Vacek could flatten even the most gnarled, off-set cobblestones of Paris-Roubaix. In a race as unpredictable as “The Hell of the North,” this type of full-frontal offense could compensate for Lidl-Trek not having a Pogi, Wout, or Mathieu.

Sadly for Lidl-Trek, multiple second-tier leaders aren’t so advantageous in grand tours, as we’re about to explore …

Ganna split from Netcompany Ineos a year early, and it seems like the British team did little to stop it from happening. According to Domestique , Netcompany Ineos didn’t demand a transfer payment from Lidl-Trek and may have even sweetened the deal.…

Pauli Blasi will race the next three seasons with Movistar. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Paula Blasi is off to Movistar on a blockbuster three-year deal to give the Spanish squad a homegrown contender to challenge the biggest names in women’s racing.

Movistar confirmed Wednesday that the 23-year-old will join from UAE Team L’IMAD in 2027 on a contract through 2029, ending months of speculation over one of the season’s most coveted signatures .

And the Spanish team is opening its wallet to make it happen.

According to MARCA , Movistar agreed to pay €85,000 to release Blasi from her UAE contract, which ran through 2027, and will pay her about €600,000 per season.

That puts its reported salary commitment above €1.8 million across three years and instantly making her one of women’s cycling’s highest-paid riders.

Movistar has not disclosed the financial terms, but Blasi’s arrival puts the Spanish team right in the middle of the race for the yellow jersey at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift .

“I’m at a point in my sporting career where I needed to take a different step and look for a team that believed in me, supported my goals and was as ambitious as I am,” Blasi said in Movistar’s official announcement.

Blasi enjoyed a breakout 2026 in only her second professional season.

She won Amstel Gold Race and then rode away with the La Vuelta Femenina to make her one of the most-prized signatures on the transfer market.

Despite some tension , she rode to fifth in her Tour de France Femmes debut while helping UAE teammate Elisa Longo Borghini reach the podium.

Now she joins Marlen Reusser and Liane Lippert in a Movistar lineup with several ways to attack the biggest races.

For Blasi, the attraction extends beyond the paycheck.

MARCA reported that UAE offered more money to retain her, but she chose Movistar after negotiations involving her agent Alex Carera , who also represents Tadej Pogačar, and team manager Sebastián Unzué.

“I’ll be able to grow, share leadership responsibilities and learn from Marlen, which will be important for my development as an athlete,” Blasi said. “And on top of that, it’s my home team. It makes me even prouder to wear the jersey.”

With Blasi, Movistar now packs a rider who could shape its women’s team for years .

Since Annemiek van Vleuten retired in 2023, the squad has worked to build another squad capable of winning across the grand tours and classics.

Blasi brings both the climbing legs and the attacking instinct to give Movistar options against rivals like Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma at the season’s biggest races .

“We are incredibly happy to finally announce Paula’s arrival on our team for the next three seasons,” Unzué said.

“Her contract represents a new step forward in terms of quality, allowing us to compete in the most important races on the calendar. I want to thank Paula for her trust and her belief in this project. We can’t wait to get started together.”

Blasi burst onto the scene in 2026 . Now for the next three years, she will be racing on the Spanish WorldTour team, and chase cycling’s biggest prizes.

And after Enric Mas won its first men’s grand tour since 2019 at La Vuelta a España, the Movistar “blues” are back.

Vollering, shown here celebrating last year, is the early favorite for the 2027 Tour de France Femmes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France Femmes will break new ground with its first team time trial, a wild opening weekend in Great Britain, and a spectacular final showdown atop the legendary Puy de Dôme.

Race director Marion Rousse unveiled a demanding nine-stage route Thursday in Paris that promises a tight the yellow jersey battle all the way to the final climb.

The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour starts July 30 in Leeds, England, and finishes August 7 atop the iconic volcano in the heart of central France.

In between, the peloton faces a punishing mix of Yorkshire hills, a historic team time trial through London, opportunities for sprinters and breakaways across northern France, and three decisive stages in the Massif Central.

In total, it’s 1,156km with 17,665m of climbing.

The route saves its biggest fireworks for last, with the Puy de Dôme set to crown the 2027 champion in a spectacular summit showdown.

As already confirmed the 2027 Tour de France Femmes opens with three stages in Great Britain, the race’s third foreign Grand Départ since its revival in 2022, following the Netherlands in 2024 and Switzerland in 2026.

The opening stage takes the peloton from Leeds to Manchester across 85.7km of rolling terrain.

Stage 2 could see an early GC shakeout, with a punishing 154.4km route from Manchester to Sheffield featuring seven categorized climbs and nearly 3,000m of climbing.

The peloton will face a team time trial for the first time since the Femmes revival in 2022.

The 18km course through London on August 1 finishes on The Mall.

After crossing the channel, racing resumes with three transition stages that give something for the sprinters and breakaways as the race hits French tarmac in northern France.

Stage 4 finishes in Calais and stage 5 in Magnanville, with both routes featuring difficult finales that could favor opportunists and puncheurs over the pure sprinters.

The fast finishers should get their best opportunity on stage 6 into Bourges, before the race turns into the gnarled roads of the Massif Central.

Stage 7 finishes atop La Loge des Gardes, the first major summit finale to open a wild final weekend.

The following day, six categorized climbs loom on the road to Clermont-Ferrand across the Massif Central.

The Puy de Dôme, one of the Tour de France’s most storied climbs, will be the battleground for the decisive final stage on August 7.

The twisting volcanic ascent returned to the men’s Tour in 2023 after a 35-year absence, with Michael Woods taking the win.

Now the women’s peloton will race up the legendary steeps overlooking Clermont-Ferrand.

Race organizers hope the battle for yellow to remain undecided until the final kilometer. The brutal slopes of the Puy de Dôme — 14.2km at 7.6% — could produce a dramatic, final-day reversal.

Who’s the course favor? On paper, defending champion Demi Vollering, as she targets a historic third Tour de France Femmes crown.

The Dutch star, who also won the 2026 world road title, can do it all on the punchy terrain and steep climbs of the Massif Central.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who joins Lidl-Trek for 2027, will be among her principal rivals, along with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot and Marlen Reusser.

Emerging star Paula Blasi, who joins Movistar, could also be a major contender after her fifth-place debut in 2026.

What’s missing? The course avoids both the Alps and the Pyrénées and the longer, sustained climbs that favor the pure climbers like Ferrand-Prévot and Niewiadoma.

Want to make Tadej Pogačar work for a record sixth Tour de France ?

Give Remco Evenepoel 71 kilometers against the clock, trim the summit finishes down to three, and deliver an old-school course without any gravel gimmicks or double assaults of Alpe d’Huez.

Perhaps that’s what ASO was thinking when the 2027 Tour de France route was unveiled Thursday in Paris with a course that some think could unsettle the world’s best cyclist.

Whether Evenepoel or anyone else can actually pull it off is another matter.

Two individual time trials in 2027 provide the most kilometers against the clock since 2012 when Bradley Wiggins won.

And with just three official summit finishes on the route, that’s fewer obvious opportunities for Pogačar to unload on his rivals.

And that presents an interesting question: Is this an anti-Pogačar Tour?

Tour officials deny they design a course in favor or against one rider’s abilities, and that also assumes anyone could design a course the Slovenian cannot conquer.

But will this Tour course give Evenepoel and others a fighting chance?

Evenepoel loves to time trial and this Tour is loaded with them.

The first is 38km from Blois to Chambord on stage 7 on a pure specialists course, followed by another 33km around Toulouse on stage 16 featuring a short ramp with 10km to go.

On paper, that should give Evenepoel — arguably the best time trialist of this generation — a huge advantage.

Both are strategically placed just before the decisive climbing blocks in the Alps and Pyrénées.

It’s the most TT miles in a Tour since Wiggins and the 2012 edition, when a prologue and two long TTs totaling just over 100km helped him win the UK’s first yellow jersey.

But how much time could Evenepoel actually take from Pogačar, who will be coming off his horrific crash at the Vuelta a España ?

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. One second per kilometer across 71km produces a cushion of 1:11. Double that and Evenepoel banks 2:22.

That’s also assuming a lot. Pogačar is no slouch against the clock, and usually gives away only a few fistfuls of seconds to Evenepoel.

Last year, he lost about 1 second per kilometer to Evenepoel in 26km late in the race when he already had yellow on ice. In 2025, when the TT came in the first week, Pogi only lost 16 seconds on 33km to Evenepoel.

But the layout for 2027 could set up an intriguing yo-yoing GC race if Pogi slightly bends the knee in the time trials.

A minute’s disadvantage would give Pogačar something to chase going into the Alps. Assuming Evenepoel can stay close, he might even be able to claw back more time and perhaps even reclaim yellow ahead of the Pyrénées.

That’s the highlight reel playing for everyone inside the Paris offices at ASO.

The bigger upside for the Belgian “aero-rocket” could come against everyone else.

Jonas Vingegaard can hold his own against the clock, but 71km gives Evenepoel a chance to build a buffer against the Dane and all the other podium contenders.

For other climbers dreaming of moving up the GC, these TT kilometers could torpedo their yellow jersey ambitions before the first week is out.

Or this Remco TT tailgate party might simply light Pogačar’s fuse to attack even more.

There’s been some grumbling that Pogačar’s relentless domination is getting boring.

Perhaps to counter that, the Tour braintrust delivered a relatively “old-school” Tour route.

There’s no first-week cobblestone stage or a hipster gravel route across the Vosges for Pogačar to smash everyone in the first week.

Even with the UK start, this is cookie-cutter stuff, with sprints and the first time trial stacked up before the Alps.

Some look to a relative dearth of summit finales with only three as evidence of another Anti-Pog bias.

It’s true that with only three true mountaintop finales, there are fewer favorable opportunities for Pogačar to crush souls. But make no mistake, Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and the Col du Portet are the real deal. It will be a huge ask for Evenepoel or anyone else to even stay close to Pogačar once he’s off the leash.

But this Tour route is harder than it looks on paper. The entire Tour route still stings with 53,450 meters of total climbing, and there are three more brutal mountain stages across the Alps, the Massif Central, and Pyrénées.

Sallanches packs 3,750 meters of climbing in a dress rehearsal for worlds. Mende stings at the end of a march across the Massif Central. And the penultimate mountain stage into Laruns delivers another 4,300 meters.

Those are massive Pogačar opportunities to make up for any lost ground.

Christian Prudhomme and company might be in for a rude surprise if they’re hoping their course will somehow muzzle Pogačar.

One can already imagine the Slovenian and UAE brass going over the race details.

Pogačar is known to attack at any point, so who’s to say he might not try to drive a split in the first week if the wind kicks up in Brittany?

It’s the other non-summit finales that could prove most pro-Pog.

Stage 10 is a dress rehearsal for the road worlds, with double-passage up and down the Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%) with 3750m of climbing with a downhill blinder to the line.

The final mountain stage to Laruns sends the race over Burdincurutcheta, Bagargui, Soudet, and Marie Blanque before the descent to the finish.

And there’s still the decisions to come on who’s racing where. Pogačar, Vingegaard, and Evenepoel all seem destined on a Tour rematch.

But perhaps more than Evenepoel, this route could favor Paul Seixas.

He can time trial as well as Pogačar and has the potential to climb even better than Evenepoel in the six mountain stages.

There are whispers that Seixas might opt to race the Giro d’Italia next year in a chance to win a grand tour, but this Tour route might tempt him back.

More than Evenepoel, this route could be ideal for Seixas to go even further than he did with fourth in his 2026 debut and perhaps even take it to Pogačar.…

Prudhomme denied the Tour de France course is designed against Pogačar. (Photo: Getty Images)

Is the 2027 Tour de France route designed to make life hard for Tadej Pogačar ?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme .

The Tour de France created a stir Thursday with its 2027 course reveal in what’s a radical departure from the past several editions .

Instead of endless uphill kickers and non-stop climbing that seemed like a red carpet for King Pog, the 114th edition is packed with two individual time trials and features only three major mountaintop finales.

Fan reaction was quick: This is an anti-Pogačar course .

Prudhomme pushed back, but didn’t hide the fact that this year’s design is far from ideal from the Slovenian superstar.

“We’ll never design a course for just one rider. Instead, we design courses for different types of riders,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio .

“We’ve done it for puncheurs for years because it’s more exciting to watch and less dangerous than a classic sprint finish. Now, we’re adding more time trials because we want to rebalance things.”

Prudhomme and the ASO braintrust are about to find out.

Two individual time trials totaling 71 kilometers, the most in 15 years, give Remco Evenepoel and rising French star Paul Seixas a chance to counter the Slovenian’s mountain firepower.

After watching Pogačar dominate the Tour since 2024 and perhaps listening to murmurs that the Slovenian’s dominance is becoming boring, the Tour race director wanted to change things up.

With the most individual time trial kilometers since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012, Tour officials are giving Evenepoel room to put his biggest advantage to work.

Rising French star Seixas also gets terrain to challenge the established order — if he decides to race the Tour.

“We have a rider who has dominated the time trial for years, Remco Evenepoel. There’s also Paul Seixas, who is very good in this discipline,” Prudhomme said. “This could be a way to rebalance the time lost in the mountains.”

Prudhomme’s explanation, though, gets to the heart of the challenge facing anyone trying to build suspense around cycling’s most dominant rider.

From the monuments to the grand tours, Pogačar has been all but unbeatable since 2024. Only a mid-race crash that ended his season cost him a likely Vuelta a España crown.

After several Tour editions of ever-increasingly difficult courses, ASO thought it was time for a change.

The start in the UK with three stages means that there won’t be a major mountain summit until the end of the first full week.

The rise of Evenepoel against the clock and Seixas’ growing all-around abilities means, that at least in the eyes of course designers, having more TT’s now makes more sense.

In earlier editions, course designers saw how Pogačar was crushing rivals both in time trials and in the mountains. Jonas Vingegaard stopped him in his tracks for two years.

“For time trials, when the same riders gain time in the mountains and in the time trial, there’s no incentive to increase the time for the individual time trials since the result is the same,” Prudhomme said.

So in that context, Prudhommme and Co. came up with a 2027 course that’s a bit of an old-school throwback.

Sprinters see more chances, including a day-one shot at yellow, and the time trial is back in vogue.

A flat 38km test through Loire château country in the first week should suit the pure specialists. The second TT just before the Pyrénées is on a 33km loop around Toulouse that features a short but steep “wall” with about 10km to go.

On paper, that could favor Evenepoel and perhaps even Seixas, whose TT chops are improving. He finished third to an unstoppable Belgian “aero-rocket” at the Montréal time trial worlds.

“It’s a clash of styles between time trial specialists who gain time in the time trial and climbers who gain time in the mountains and lose it in the time trial,” he said.

Prudhomme called the Col du Portet the Tour’s “new Tourmalet” and said the final mountain stages in the Pyrénées will prove decisive.

“This could turn the tables 48 hours before the final arrival in Paris,” he said. “We want to keep the suspense going for as long as possible.”

But will the Tour makeover work and keep the tension in the race all the way to the final weekend?

“It’s not an anti-Pogačar strategy,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio . “Pogačar loves challenges. So, he might be the one to win both time trials.”

So much for finding a chink in the Slovenian’s armor.

Pogačar will like what he sees in the 2027 Tour de France route. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France is going big on time trials and short on summit finales with its historic return to Great Britain.

Race director Christian Prudhomme unveiled the 114th edition Thursday in Paris, confirming a 3,479km route from Edinburgh to the Champs-Élysées from July 2-25.

The numbers tell the story: 21 stages, 53,450 meters of climbing, six mountain stages but only three summit finales, and two individual time trials totaling 71km, the most since 2012.

Can Remco Evenepoel dare to dream of yellow? Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard still might have the last word in this deceptively challenging course.

The race opens with three stages across Scotland, England, and Wales before returning to France via Normandy.

Then things get serious. The first week closes with the first of two time trials before driving into the Alps.

Three summit finishes await at Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and the monstrous Col du Portet in the Pyrénées in the final week.

That’s low by modern standards but these all pack an over-sized bite. There are three other mountain stages that don’t end at a summit but are still loaded with race-breaking climbs.

The Alps also include two ascents of the Côte de Domancy, a preview of the 2027 world championships course in a stage that could explode the GC.

The decisive final week packs in another time trial before the Pyrénées, a brutal Tourmalet and Col du Portet double, and a final mountain showdown to Laruns.

And the favorites? It’s shaping up to be a blockbuster.

Pogačar and Vingegaard will be looking to return to their best after injury setbacks, while rising stars Isaac del Toro and Paul Seixas could elbow in if they race.

The generous time trial distance — the most since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012 — should give Evenepoel favorable terrain, but he will still have to survive the mountain onslaught.

The Tour wraps up July 25 with loops over the dramatic Montmartre climb — yes, it’s back with three passages — before the traditional Champs-Élysées finale.

What’s missing? Iconic climbs like Alpe d’Huez or Mont Ventoux and the race barely touches the Massif Central.

Sprinters will see plenty of chances, with perhaps up to seven sprints, including the penultimate stage that gives the fast men a reason to suffer over the Pyrénées.

With 71km against the clock and a string of monster climbs, the 2027 Tour looks set to reward the complete rider.

"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.…

Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.

But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.

Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.

But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries?

One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate.

The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.

On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries.

And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes.

If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.

Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care

State pension likely to top £13,000 a year

What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?

But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows.

However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.

So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK?

Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund.

But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.

Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.

And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes).

Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing.

As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.

So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap.

The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.

It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men.

But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.

Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.

So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere.

But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action.

The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.

That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.

PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.

But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.

AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.

It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.

The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.

That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.

Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.

A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.

Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.

More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.

Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.

Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.

"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".

Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X.

"If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.

Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems.

E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.

The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.

The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can.

"Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said.

"The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.

Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.

The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.

The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

"Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.

Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.

The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said.

The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors.

"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.

The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.…

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.…

The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people".

The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border.

The White House, in a statement, said that starting 30 October the US would remove certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.

It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others .

The White House said the action reflects President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade", as well as "offsetting the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada's discriminatory treatment".

The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment.

Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC.

Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

So far, Canada has not commented on the White House's announcement.

LeBlanc's office did not immediately respond on Friday to the BBC's request for comment.

The Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.

The reductions could be offset by raising levies on ​other Canadian goods, the Journal reported.

In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X.

Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.

​Maine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.

Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties.

The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks.

With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month.

The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren.

From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life.

"I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom.

She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older.

"They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes."

Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren.

Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok."

On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff.

She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits.

Now she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves.

"I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that."

She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five.

Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad".

Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective.

She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign.

"I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand."

Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium".

Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades.

Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job.

Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off.

"I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says.

Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table".

Baker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world".

Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says.

That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts.

Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had".

"Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy."

Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on.

She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children.

"It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life."

On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

The pace of UK price rises accelerated ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The rate of inflation rose to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continued to squeeze global oil supplies.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

The wars in the middle east and Ukraine have pushed up fuel prices. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."

He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field .

The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".

The figures came as the ONS said the government borrowed £25bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.

A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs says he was ''surprised'' to have been charged with fraud.

Kashim Chowdhury told the jury at Southwark Crown Court he had not been dishonest in failing to tell his employers he had other government jobs.

"At that time I was just on auto pilot, I was like a robot, I was not thinking clearly," he said.

Chowdhury, 55, from east London, is accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight overlapping public sector jobs. He was contractually obliged to work full time and was paid a full-time salary by each organisation. He is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000.

In March 2023 Chowdhury began working for the Home Office despite being under contract to work full time at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.

The court was told he started the Home Office job while on sick leave from three of his other jobs.

Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ asked him: "If you were really sick for work, how were you able to start your work at the Home Office?"

Chowdhury said: "I did not want this job at the Home Office, I was told there would be adequate support and I could work whatever hours I wanted to work."

Organ also asked why he did not submit a sick note to the Home Office "You were using these sick notes to be able to cope. It was all too much wasn't it?"

Chowdhury rejected the suggestion, adding: "I wanted to carry on working."

In May 2023, Chowdhury was contracted to work 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.

He told the jury he agreed with his employers to work flexibly and that his work was project or output based. He said this was agreed "informally" via text messages but the phones used to send the texts had gone missing when his house was searched by investigators.

He said that to cope with the workload he would work from 07:00 on Saturdays and Sundays and not finish until 20:00 or 21:00.

Organ asked him: "Wasn't that a bit much for you?"

"I was house bound, I was looking after my mum," he said.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".

His line manager at the UKHSA, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023 to discuss his sick leave.

She previously told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.

She told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."

But Chowdhury denied having worn make-up at the meeting

''That's a smear, I've never worn make-up in my life. At that particular time, I was suffering from anxiety and depression. I had already submitted my sick note, there was no need to put on make-up.''
